comments.body: I imagine a major reason for the decline of labor's share of wealth is the shifting nature of labor. What does a worker, say in a factory, actually 'do', and what is that activity's contribution to wealth creation? There was a time when (Western) factories made products. A washing machine company made washing machines by transforming sheets of metal and rolls of copper wire and some other stuff into a functioning domestic apparatus. Today a washing machine is essentially the result of a logistical process in which an array of components coming from elsewhere, usually East Asia, is briefly warehoused and then presented for assembly into a finished product. That is to say, the value added by the assembly process is significantly lower than what the true crafting used to add. To supplement that effect, there is the virtually maximized automation and digitalization that have happened over the past 50 years, and that have moved skills and expertise into machines. What this also means, obviously, is that what is sold as increased worker productivity is nothing of the sort. The output per hour worked has seemingly multiplied, but not because workers have become better at their jobs. In reality a lot of the work is still being done, only off site, where components are made, and the rest of the gain is due to work having been handed off to machines.

I was in 4th grade on 9/11. School started at 9 AM, and every morning before class started the teacher would turn on the local news and let us watch, so that we would become good citizens knowing what was going on the world. That morning the whole class was being super rowdy, and I distinctly remember the teacher yelling “Everybody be quiet, the news is important!” She had no idea what had just happened and turned on the TV. The whole class saw the burning towers and sat there in silence. Then the teacher looked horrified and turned off the TV. 

The principal walked in to our class 10 minutes later and made us swear not to tell anyone else in the school the rest of the day. We had to pretend everything was normal when we all knew something terrible had happened. 

I remember looking up at the sky during recess, processing it all, and seeing how blue it was. To this day, when I see a sky like that I still call it 9/11 blue.

Before and After

Before September 11, 2001, security was largely invisible. 

You could arrive at the airport 30 minutes before departure with family at the gate. No shoes off, no laptops out, no body scanners. A water bottle or pocket knife drew no attention. Office buildings, courthouses, and stadiums required only a ticket or a signature in a logbook. Travel was anonymous.

That ease reflected a quiet belief that we were safe here, insulated by oceans.

I watched the second plane hit live, watched the towers fall, and watched ash-covered people walk uptown for hours. We all knew someone who knew someone. 2,977 people went to work that morning and never came home.

Afterward, the nation changed fundamentally to ensure it never happened again. The Department of Homeland Security was created. Private airport security was replaced by the TSA. Cockpit doors were reinforced. 

What feels routine today felt jarring then, because we remember what it cost to require it.

While I think the Atlantic’s article “The End of Reading” is exaggerating, I was dumbstruck by the poor capacity of some of them to read and write. When I went over to the place of one of them, I thought he must have been babysitting because there was a little kid’s writing taped to the door. Turned out that was the handwriting of a full grown man. He didn’t know how to spell words like “Lutheran” despite claiming this was his religion. His defense for these were that he didn’t usually need to write and could rely on autocorrect. One told me she struggled to get through a paragraph of a book sometimes so would ask ChatGPT what it meant, and most of her emails at work would be written by AI. Although the lost need for skills when we have tech to do it for us is understandable and should stymie fears of any sort of economic collapse, the tech is also clearly severely hampering the capacity of people to learn. It seems like an acceleration of a problem; my parents and grandparents would watch Shakespeare plays I’d struggle to understand, trounce me at Scrabble, write beautiful cursive in letters without ever a need to scratch out a word, and devour NYT crosswords when I’d be lucky to ever be able to answer a question…without the use of my phone.

Even within these countries, more tech use correlates to lower student performance. Meanwhile in the U.S., the majority of public schools have a "one to one" Chromebook allocation and most middle and high school students carry around devices all day and do most of their homework on a device, while elementary school students are taught by a giant digital whiteboard on which YouTube videos are often playing. If we don't address this massive elephant in the room, we're not going to see a reversal of this trend anytime soon. The ripple effects of this across society is too terrifying to contemplate, but we must contemplate it. 

Betsy Tao
Distraction Free Schools Maryland

comments.name: J P Tristani

"...suggests plane may have been approaching Miami’s airport too fast" .... ".."Publicly available flight data plane’s speed was 112 knots—about 129 miles an hour—as it left the usable area of the runway, according to aviation tracker Flightradar24."

Both are not accurate for a preliminary report on the B767 speed and was not stated at the NTSB report I watched yesterday, Monday.  Only the FDR (Flight Data Recorder) would give such speeds, and they were recovered and sent to NTSB HQ for review.

The important part of the NTSB investigation will be B767 touchdown point on Runway 30/9000 ft, usually 800 ft beyond threshold leaving more than 8000 ft to stop; the approach speed normally at 30% above stall speed (increasing with a/c weight, wind direction and gust added)

--usually, 1/2 the steady wind and all the gusts.  The wind was from 190 deg, 20 mph with gusts up to 30 mph, giving a slight left tailwind less than 10 mph.   Weather is a factor with rain, but R30 has transverse grooving to prevent standing water lessening any tire hydroplaning.

On touchdown, it becomes pilot technique of no flare, power above idle for quick spool up if go-around needed, keeping the nose heading down the centerline, wing spoilers extended to reduce wing lift (more tire friction on runway), Main and Nose gear on runway, reverse thrust up to maximum of 50% available, and application of braking up to max ABS.

NTSB has to determine what happened throughout that sequence that resulted in the overrun.

The “firewall” against the AfD should be understood in the context of German history. The AfD says it has no intention of dismantling the German basic law, the Grundgesetz. But constitutional safeguards cannot depend solely upon political assurances.

Germany experienced two World Wars between 1914 and 1945, followed by extraordinary destruction and human loss. The lesson drawn from that catastrophe was not simply to hope that history would not repeat itself, but to construct institutions capable of resisting the forces that had destroyed Germany’s first democracy.

The Grundgesetz was ratified in May 1949. Its constitutional architecture reflects the principle of “Nie wieder” — Never Again.

From that perspective, a political firewall is not necessarily an assault on democracy. It can instead be understood as one of the mechanisms by which Germany’s post-war democracy protects the constitutional order that was deliberately created after 1945.

The question is therefore not whether the AfD should be silenced. It is whether Germany should ignore the historical reasons why its democratic system contains safeguards against precisely this kind of political danger.

I felt a little miffed when my midwestern city adopted these, imposing a one-time charge to do so.  

I have changed my mind.  

It is vastly better for sanitation workers and their backs, and for residents who have no business trying to wrestle or carry a traditional trash can to curbside.  It might have kept my father from fracturing his pelvis from
Trying to stand on one leg and stomp the trash down in the trash can.

And while New Yorker’s may be used to tat populations comparable to London during the Plague, it is a bad idea.  

We see rats infrequently in my city.  Raccoons can sometimes get in.

When our Civil War vintage elm was still with us, we did have squirrel(s) who would invest a couple years time to gnaw through the lid so as to have a winter buffet.  

After he managed to get in, a call to city sanitation got us another lid.

But for a year after that, the squirrel would be sit in “V” in the elm, looking through my living room window, glaring at me for negating his hard work.

Adopt these trash bins, and the rats will not be happy.

I am not that empathic.  I worry more about disease than the opinions of ten million rats and their disease-carrying fellow travellers.  I still recommend the bins.

So much of this phenomenon seems tied to changes in media.

We have gone from an era in which people got most of their political information from network news and newspapers to one in which the primary source is more often social media posts and podcasts. 

In the Before Times, what we called the mainstream media was motivated by a desire to appeal to as many people as possible, which meant presenting issues in a balanced way that could retain credibility with a broad audience. Also, print and broadcast media faced actual legal requirements to present news in a balanced way, and consequences for not doing so.

The current, fragmented media environment, the angriest and most extreme voices are those most likely to be heard. There is little, if any, drawback to presenting news that is inaccurate or even blatantly false. Libel and slander don't apply online.

And it turns out that, given the choice, consumers will avoid news reports that challenge their values and viewpoints, and patronize sources that tell them what they want to hear. 

Thus it becomes possible for about one third of the American public to live in a world where Biden stole the 2020 election, climate change is a hoax, immigrants are eating your cats and dogs, and school districts are plotting to give your children sex change operations, while another third feels obligated to stand up against such madness, and the final third seemingly can't decide which version of reality they should buy into.

The lead up to the Great Depression.  The 1960’s (Vietnam war, civil rights, etc).  Conversely- there have been times of relative calm when the pendulum barely moved at all (post World War II).  The Eisenhower presidency was hugely popular, because the difference between the democrats and the republicans was small.  Congress actually functioned with consensus.

The current predicament can be traced back to Nixon, and became progressively worse with each passing decade.  The two political parties became more and more entrenched.  Voters are/were presented  with an either/or approach to every issue.  Of course- as we all know- not every subject is so cut and dry.  There are many shades of gray. Everything is:  “take no prisoners.”  Add to that the fact that- due to the internet- everyone lives in an echo chamber.  

I don’t see a way out of this without a complete overhaul and rejection of the two-party system.  Until we come up with a better system, the pendulum will continue to swing wildly from left to right.

The defining mark of a declining political culture is not fierce disagreement, but the loss of nuance. Contemporary political life has flattened into rigid binaries—left versus right, good versus bad—that replace critical thinking with tribal alignment. When every policy dilemma becomes a zero-sum contest, the intellectual habits required for self-governance vanish. Democratic citizenship depends on a commitment to complexity, shared evidence, and the recognition that public problems rarely yield simplistic solutions. Modern polling and partisan discourse enforce this reductionism, coercing citizens to align rather than deliberate. 

Consider the debate over immigration pit absolute openness against total restriction, ignoring the foundational tension between a nation-state's need for defined borders and its moral duties toward non-citizens. These issues cannot be resolved by partisan slogans; they demand history, law, and reasoned inquiry. 

A healthy republic requires a Socratic disposition: asking "What evidence supports your conclusion?" rather than "Which side are you on?" Without a shared baseline of logic and empirical reality, public conversation devolves into noise and tribal hostility. Sustaining democracy demands resisting instant reactions, refusing false binaries, and choosing instead to ask better questions.

Studies show behaviours and conditions of life of our grandparents effect our epigenetics. This is not heredity as we understand it, but an imprinting of the life and circumstances of parents, grandparents, and probably beyond, though the signals get too weak to find. Parents have a responsibility to be as fit and healthy and live as healthy a life as possible in order to give the best chances to their offspring.

comments.body: Fantastic article about our attitudes towards living even while being surrounded by the certainty of being mortal. My late father built his dream home on the property that his father-in-law gave him as a wedding gift. He started building on it in 1980 when I was just 14. It was a nice piece of land surrounded by trees but uniquely had a large cemetery right behind our back yard. You could see the tombstones from the windows of the master bedroom and our main bathroom. And to make it really quite interesting many of the German ancestors and relatives on my maternal grandparents were buried there dating back to the mid 19th century. A lot of my teenage experiences were tied up with that place. I first learned how to roll a joint near the Memorial cenotaph and knew a lot of kids who would hang out and even make out after night fell. Interestingly our house was located on the top of a hill just minutes away from the Monroeville Mall where George Romero filmed his 1979 classic Dawn of the Dead; you could see it from the picture windows in our living room in the front of the house. I used to torment my kid brother who was afraid of zombies by first saying that they didn't exist at all, but if they actually do remember that we're well situated on ground zero with our late relatives just minutes away. Needless to say that didn't help.

My approach to learning new words:

Primarily, I try to understand a word’s etymology and look for words that use its roots and stems.

Next, I’ll look at a word’s secondary meanings. ‘Tertiary’, for example, usually means third in rank, but it also describes higher, university education or advanced medical care.

Lastly, I tap tertiary sentence-writing tactics: using rhyme or writing flash fiction.

Primarily, I aim to improve my thinking skills, secondarily to build my vocabulary, and tertiarily to connect with fellow students, writers, and journalists through The New York Times.

Although the report is ostensibly about the destruction, loss, and suffering experienced by people on the Tibetan side of the border as a result of the recent disaster, it never cites, quotes, or even mentions a single Tibetan—a native of the land. There is only Tibet, the land, but no Tibetans. Instead, the people quoted and mentioned are exclusively those with Chinese names.
How did it come to this?
One cannot understand the situation without acknowledging the historical and political context: the Chinese People’s Liberation Army (PLA) entered Tibet in 1950, and Tibet has been under Chinese control ever since. The Chinese presence in Tibet is not simply that of ordinary residents; it is the result of a contested political and military occupation. Yet this article presents that presence as entirely normal, without mentioning the fundamental historical context.

comments.name: Camille
comments.body: I understand your interest in this place, understand your affection. Not every place needs to be spectacular, or even perfect, all the time. A favorite restaurant of mine in Philly is uneven. What keeps me there is a combination of things, including the atmosphere and the workers. The food, too, yes. It’s good, but I’ve learned what not to order. I've also learned not to recommend it to others, at least not without warnings. If I stumbled into Somssi in bad weather, I suspect I’d also be happy. On a lovely day, however? I’m a little less certain. There are as of today 13 items on the menu. The hit or miss ratio is therefore more important than at a place with 2 dozen choices. I agree with your assessment that it’s not-so-expensive (the fine print says “expensive”), but some items are quite pricey. And that matters when some are just fine, some are not, and others are wonderful. It shrinks one’s options. It is worthwhile to showcase good restaurants. A consideration, though, that I think should always matter is consistency. A restaurant in which some things are good, if not wonderful, and some things are forgettable can be a nice standby in the right circumstances. Like my Philly place. A restaurant in which everything is good and some things are wonderful is a better standby. A place worth meeting friends at. Perhaps in the future you can report if Somssi has become that standby. I hope it does, because it seems as if it should. In time, that is.

comments.body: With all the rampant star-flation in restaurant ratings online, I wanted to remind everyone: For us, one star is still GOOD. It means this is a place where you can spend a delightful evening. There may be only a couple of truly standout dishes. But some nights it’s enough to be with friends in a relaxed, not-too-expensive spot that, in an increasingly cookie-cutter world, has genuine personality and warmth. Shouldn’t we recognize these restaurants too?

This is such an interesting story and feels very much of a piece with other fights where unquantified and non-maximized but evidently sustainable practices by local historical residents is being displaced by corporations interested in extraction for maximal profits but with uncertain impacts for the future of the resource. Here it’s the seaweed; but this story has been told over and over again, especially in fisheries where populations are more fluid. 

I’m really curious about the current sustainability of the seaweed harvests in this area - and to see the cultural and ecological implications of increased industrial activity in this system. It will also be interesting to see if there is any real local resistance, and if so what form it might take. Good find NYT!

comments.name: Nick Wright
comments.body:
It's important to note that Canada's government is carefully targeting its tariffs at US products where there alternatives Canadians can buy from other sources, both Canadian and from other exporting countries. In other words, we don't have to pay the tariffs on US exports; we can acquire the same or similiar goods untariffed elsewhere. The impact of our tariffs will therefore mainly affect American exporters, whose products Canadians will no longer be buying.

That's the difference between how a responsible government uses tariffs and how an irresponsible government uses them: Trump is hurting American exporters and consumers as much or more than he's hurting Canadians.

I've been to Taiwan, and the food is amazing for non-vegetarians. Beef noodle soup is the national dish and executed to perfection. The food court in the basement of Taipei 101 is excellent.

comments.name: Chuck
comments.body: If Ms. Kung were to revisit Taipei next week, I'd recommend she walk into some of the local traditional markets there. One particular market stands out, the Di What Street market. It's the most popular market for local residents to do their shopping for the lunar New Year holiday. It's got a puppet museum and a temple along side with numerous teahouses and restaurants stretching over a street that's 500 meters long at least, not to mention all the winding and narrow alleys running through it. Best of all, visitors can find all kinds of fabrics in the main public building of the market. You can spend an afternoon there going up and down the three-story building hunting for the fabrics that delights you and have it made into the final handkerchief or whatever shape you want to take it back home as a souvenir. You can also have it embroiled with your name on it while you have your oolong or latte inside the same building.

Not only was there no inherent rush or hurry to do certain things, but I could also  enjoy the day and relax the whole time, or maybe pick up a new skill and try something new. The freedom of that was something I took for granted. Sure summer was fun and all but beyond that, I thought I had learned a bit about who I was as a  person. Spending time with family, and coming to know about our family history;meeting new people, it was really eye-opening. All in all, I’m excited that this summer was great, and I’m looking forward to fall.
